title: Virtue en Vogue
author: Abadal, Lily
source: Wisdom in the Machine Age (wisdominthemachineage.substack.com), September 10, 2026
summary: The piece is a personal essay by philosopher-educator Lily Abadal built around a convocation speech she gave to high schoolers in 2021, unearthed by accident among her disorganized voice-memo notes. Her central argument is a virtue-ethics account of authenticity: the popular notion of 'being true to yourself' is incoherent because it treats momentary desires as fixed and never asks whether those desires are good. She proposes replacing that ideal with being 'true to the process' — a three-step program of identifying a positive ideal of character, honestly naming one's flaws, and embracing the discomfort of moral effort as intrinsic to becoming virtuous rather than a sign one is on the wrong path. The essay frames virtue as something trained the way an athlete trains a body, and treats struggle itself as diagnostic of growth rather than evidence of a mismatch. Read today, on a Substack devoted to human formation in an AI-saturated age, the 2021 speech becomes evidence for Abadal's broader thesis that character education is newly urgent now that AI is exposing how much human development was being neglected. The piece is unusual for using a decade-old text as a time capsule showing a stable core of belief.
points: Reframes the 'be yourself' cliché as a category error: it never asks whether the self you're being true to is good, or whether your loves have simply not yet matured.
Offers 'be true to the process' as a replacement ideal — naming an ideal, admitting flaws, and treating difficulty as the normal cost of building virtue.
Uses the analogy of physical training (swinging a bat) to argue moral and intellectual formation take comparably deliberate repetition, not natural inclination.
Insists real authenticity requires the courage to look honestly at your own shortcomings rather than the comfort of excusing them as 'just who I am.'
Positions the whole argument as recognizably Aristotelian even though it was delivered as an ordinary high-school assembly talk.
quotes: But that concept misses two very important very things. It fails to ask the question if any of these things are good!?! What if you just don't apologize to people because it's something you don't want to do?

So, today, Barons I want to make a suggestion…instead of using the phrase to true to yourself, I suggest that we try to be true to the process. The process of what??? The process of becoming the best version of you.
Admit your flaws. And weakness. Admit where you aren't hitting the mark. Not as a means of shaming yourself, but as a means of inspiring yourself.
Every path to virtue is hard. As we become better at things and as we come to understand them more we like them more. That's how we are wired.
If you have to train your body to perfect the act of swinging a bat for hours and hours and hours, how much time do you think is required to train your heart, to train your mind?
Being truly and really authentic is a process and it takes time. Because it's a virtue. It's not the cheap notion of just latching onto and living in our flaws and current preferences and desires.
It's where your actions, and your desires, your heart and your mind all align with what is good for you as a human being. Be true to the process.
